paras: The Vincinnes Hotel kitchen fight was a clash between white cooks and Black waiters in the kitchen of the "Vincinnes Hotel" in Chicago on a Sunday morning in early August 1900, apparently August 5, after the cooks tried to beat a waiter named James Meadows. Several people were cut or struck, the kitchen was wrecked, and police took fifteen hotel employees away in a patrol wagon. The Indianapolis Freeman, the only paper found to report it, called the fight a "race riot."

According to the Freeman, the cooks at the hotel had been "quite abusive to the waiters for some time" before the fight. Meadows had "gained the displeasure of the cooks," who then set out to beat him.

Meadows "had friends among the waiters," who joined the fight, and the paper wrote that when it ended "the colored boys had successfully bombarded the fort." The chef, E. Weston, had part of his lip cut off, and the steward, L.H. Smith, was hit over the left eye with a large projectile. Flying missiles cut Anna Zartimes, and a razor wielded by one of the waiters struck down Joseph Coleman, described as a "white dishwasher." Meadows himself was "badly cut up," and broken china and glassware lay piled in every corner of the wrecked kitchen.

The police patrol arrived at the end of the fight, and fifteen employees of the hotel were "given a free ride." The account does not name those taken or report any charges, and no report of a court hearing was found.

The fight appears only in a brief in the Indianapolis Freeman of August 11, 1900, on page 3, and no white-press account was found. The Freeman told the story in sporting and military language, calling it a "battle royal" in which the waiters "won the victory." It closed with a mixed editorial line: "While we condem and regret occurrences like the above, we are glad to know that the colored boys won."

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Indianapolis Freeman)
accounts.gist: The white cooks had long abused the Black waiters and tried to beat James Meadows; the waiters came to his aid and 'won the victory', leaving the kitchen wrecked and several people cut before police took fifteen employees away.

framing.detail: The Freeman described the fight as a 'battle royal' and 'race riot' in which the waiters 'bombarded the fort', said it condemned and regretted such occurrences, but was 'glad to know that the colored boys won'.

record_check.dossier: Attempted beating, fight with missiles and a razor, kitchen wrecked; no one was reported killed, so 'killing' is unsupported

record_check.record: James Meadows, Anna Zartimes, Joseph Coleman, E. Weston, L.H. Smith
record_check.dossier: Meadows was the target of the attack; Weston, Smith, Zartimes and Coleman were injured in the fight (Coleman by a waiter's razor) and are injured parties, not targets
Meadows was one of the 'colored' waiters (implied by the account)
Co-workers (the cooks) in a workplace fight
At least 1 stated (Joseph Coleman, 'white dishwasher'); chef Weston, steward Smith and Anna Zartimes also injured, race not stated
'Last Sunday morning' relative to the August 11 issue; August 5 is inferred, not printed

info: 'Last Sunday morning' before the Saturday, August 11, 1900 issue, i.e. Sunday, August 5, 1900 (inferred from the issue date)
Kitchen of the 'Vincinnes Hotel' (as printed), Chicago
James Meadows, a waiter, whom the cooks 'undertook to beat up'; he was 'badly cut up'
The white cooks of the hotel, said to have been 'quite abusive to the waiters for some time'

sources.note: Only report found: white cooks at the 'Vincinnes Hotel', Chicago, tried to beat waiter James Meadows 'last Sunday morning'; Black waiters fought back; chef, steward, a woman and a white dishwasher injured, Meadows 'badly cut up'; fifteen employees taken in the police patrol; editor glad 'the colored boys won'.
quotes: It seems that the cooks of the Vincinnes have been quite abusive to the waiters for some time which culminated in a race riot.
A waiter by the name of James Meadows gained the displeasure of the cooks and they undertook to beat him up
a razor wielded by one of the waiters laid Joseph Coleman, white dishwasher, in the shade.
While we condem and regret occurrences like the above, we are glad to know that the colored boys won.
